title: What are Flink windows (tumbling / sliding / session / global, count-based vs time-based) and their components (assigner, trigger, evictor), and what is a watermark (a logical event-time marker, watermark = max_event_ts − max_out_of_order_delay, e.g. forBoundedOutOfOrderness) used to trigger windows and handle out-of-order/late events?
shortTitle: What are Flink windows and watermarks

s1_definition.profdef: A Flink window is a mechanism that groups an unbounded stream of events into finite buckets so that an aggregation function can run over each bucket. Tumbling windows are fixed-size and non-overlapping, sliding windows are fixed-size but overlap by a slide interval, session windows close after a gap of inactivity, and global windows collect everything until a custom trigger fires. A watermark is a special marker that flows with the stream and asserts that event time has progressed to a certain point, so that time-based windows know when they can safely close and emit a result even though events may arrive slightly out of order.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants to count how many transactions Rajesh makes every one minute. The clock on each transaction is the time it actually happened at the ATM, not the time it reached the server. A tumbling window is like dividing the day into back-to-back one-minute slots and counting transactions in each slot. A sliding window is like a security guard who every ten seconds looks back over the last minute. A session window is like saying "a shopping session ends when Rajesh does nothing for five minutes." The watermark is the bank manager announcing "it is now safely 10:01, any transaction stamped before 10:01 should have arrived by now, so close the 10:00-to-10:01 slot and publish the count."
s1_definition.oneliner: A window slices the endless stream into countable buckets, and a watermark is the clock that tells each bucket when it is safe to close.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Flink window is a mechanism that groups an unbounded stream of events into finite buckets so that an aggregation function can run over each bucket. Tumbling windows are fixed-size and non-overlapping, sliding windows are fixed-size but overlap by a slide interval, session windows close after a gap of inactivity, and global windows collect everything until a custom trigger fires. A watermark is a special marker that flows with the stream and asserts that event time has progressed to a certain point, so that time-based windows know when they can safely close and emit a result even though events may arrive slightly out of order.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India wants to count how many transactions Rajesh makes every one minute. The clock on each transaction is the time it actually happened at the ATM, not the time it reached the server. A tumbling window is like dividing the day into back-to-back one-minute slots and counting transactions in each slot. A sliding window is like a security guard who every ten seconds looks back over the last minute. A session window is like saying "a shopping session ends when Rajesh does nothing for five minutes." The watermark is the bank manager announcing "it is now safely 10:01, any transaction stamped before 10:01 should have arrived by now, so close the 10:00-to-10:01 slot and publish the count."

**One line to remember:** A window slices the endless stream into countable buckets, and a watermark is the clock that tells each bucket when it is safe to close.

sections.s2_technical:
Windows in Flink come in two broad families. Time-based windows group events by event time or processing time, and count-based windows group by a fixed number of elements. The four shapes are tumbling, sliding, session, and global. A tumbling window of one minute produces non-overlapping slots: `stream.keyBy(t -> t.accountId).window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1)))`. A sliding window has a size and a slide, so `SlidingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1), Time.seconds(10))` emits a one-minute view every ten seconds and an event can belong to several windows. A session window closes after a gap: `EventTimeSessionWindows.withGap(Time.minutes(5))`. A global window puts everything in one window and relies entirely on a custom trigger, `GlobalWindows.create()`.

Every window has three internal components. The window assigner decides which window or windows an incoming element belongs to. The trigger decides when the window function actually fires and produces output, for example `EventTimeTrigger` fires when the watermark passes the window end, `CountTrigger` fires after N elements, and `ProcessingTimeTrigger` fires on the wall clock. The evictor is optional and can remove elements from the window buffer before or after the function runs, which is useful for keeping only the last few records.

A watermark is the heart of event-time processing. Event streams arrive out of order because of network delays and retries, so Flink needs a way to decide "I have probably seen all events up to time T." A watermark of T means exactly that. You usually generate watermarks with a bounded-out-of-orderness strategy: `WatermarkStrategy.forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(5))` sets the watermark to the maximum event timestamp seen so far minus five seconds, which tolerates up to five seconds of lateness. When the watermark crosses a window's end time, the `EventTimeTrigger` fires that window. Events that arrive after the watermark has already passed their window are late; by default they are dropped, but you can keep windows open with allowed lateness or route late events to a side output. The senior nuance is that watermark lag directly trades latency against completeness: a larger out-of-orderness delay waits longer and catches more late events but adds latency, while a smaller one emits faster but drops more.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India the fraud team wants a running count of how many transactions each account performs in every one-minute slot, because a sudden burst of transactions in one minute is a classic card-testing fraud signal. The transactions carry the time they happened at the point of sale, and because of mobile network delays they do not arrive in perfect order. If the bank simply counted by arrival time, a transaction that happened at 10:00:59 but arrived at 10:01:02 would be counted in the wrong minute and the fraud math would be wrong. This is exactly what event-time tumbling windows plus watermarks solve: the window groups by the real transaction time, and the watermark decides when the minute is safely complete.

Problem 2 — A few transactions arrive very late, for example a payment stamped 10:00:30 that only reaches the server at 10:02 because the customer's phone was offline. If we close the 10:00 window the instant the watermark passes, that late payment is lost from the count. We want to still account for a small amount of lateness. This is exactly the bounded-out-of-orderness watermark plus allowed lateness, where the watermark lags the maximum seen time by a few seconds so slightly-late events still land in the right window.

In the mini-project we build a small runnable demo that does not need a Flink cluster but faithfully reproduces the logic. We create a `Transaction` record with an account id, amount, and event timestamp. A `TumblingWindowCounter` assigns each transaction to its one-minute window based on event time. A `WatermarkGenerator` tracks the maximum seen timestamp and computes the watermark as max minus the out-of-orderness delay. A `WindowTriggerEngine` fires a window only once the watermark has passed its end, emitting the per-account count, and routes events that arrive after their window has already fired into a late side output. A `FraudWindowDemo` main class feeds an out-of-order stream of Rajesh and Priya transactions, prints which window each lands in, shows a window firing when the watermark crosses it, and shows one genuinely late event going to the side output.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  window:
    size-seconds: 60            # tumbling window length
    out-of-orderness-seconds: 5 # watermark lag tolerated
    allowed-lateness-seconds: 0 # extra grace after watermark passes
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a stream of seven transactions for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), with event times ranging from 10:00:05 to 10:01:30, deliberately out of order, with a window size of one minute and an out-of-orderness tolerance of five seconds.

Step 1: The first transaction for Rajesh at 10:00:05 arrives. The watermark generator records the max seen time as 5s, so the watermark is 5s minus 5s equals 0s. The window start is the floor of 5s to the minute, which is 10:00:00, and the window end is 10:01:00. The watermark (0s) is far below the window end, so the event is accepted into the 10:00 window. Count for Rajesh in that window becomes one.

Step 2: Rajesh at 10:00:15 and Priya at 10:00:20 arrive. Both fall into the same 10:00-to-10:01 window for their own account. Rajesh's count in the 10:00 window becomes two, Priya's becomes one. The max seen advances to 20s, watermark to 15s, still below the 10:01:00 end, so nothing fires.

Step 3: Rajesh at 10:00:59 arrives even though it is out of order relative to what comes next. It still belongs to the 10:00 window because 59s floors to 10:00:00. Rajesh's 10:00 window count becomes three. Max seen is 59s, watermark 54s, still below 10:01:00.

Step 4: Rajesh at 10:01:01 arrives. It floors into the next window, 10:01:00 to 10:02:00. Max seen becomes 61s, watermark becomes 56s, which is still below the 10:00 window end of 60s, so the 10:00 window still does not fire yet.

Step 5: Priya at 10:01:30 arrives. Max seen jumps to 90s, so the watermark becomes 85s. Now the watermark has crossed the 10:00 window end of 60s. The trigger engine fires every 10:00 window: Rajesh fires with count three and the sum of 1200 plus 300 plus 450, and Priya fires with count one.

Step 6: Finally a very late Rajesh transaction stamped 10:00:30 arrives. Its window is 10:00, whose end is 60s, but the current watermark is already 85s, which is past 60s. The window already fired, so this event is late. The engine routes it to the late side output instead of corrupting the already-published count.

Final output:

```

2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Accepted SAV2001 amount 300.00 into window [0,60000)
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Accepted CUR3001 amount 9000.00 into window [0,60000)
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Accepted SAV2001 amount 450.00 into window [0,60000)
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Accepted SAV2001 amount 75.00 into window [60000,120000)
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] WINDOW FIRED account=SAV2001 window=[0,60000) count=3 total=1950.00
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] WINDOW FIRED account=CUR3001 window=[0,60000) count=1 total=9000.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Flink window is how you turn an endless, unbounded stream into finite buckets that an aggregation can run over. There are four shapes. A tumbling window chops time into fixed, non-overlapping slots like back-to-back one-minute buckets. A sliding window is a fixed-size view that advances by a smaller slide, so it overlaps and one event can land in several windows. A session window groups bursts of activity and closes after a configurable gap of inactivity. A global window puts everything into one window and relies entirely on a custom trigger. Windows can also be count-based instead of time-based. Internally every window has three parts: an assigner that decides which window an event belongs to, a trigger that decides when the window fires and produces output, and an optional evictor that can drop elements from the buffer.

The piece that makes event-time windows correct is the watermark. Streams arrive out of order because of network delays and retries, so Flink needs a principled way to say "I have probably now seen everything up to time T." A watermark is exactly that assertion flowing through the pipeline. The common strategy is bounded out of orderness, where the watermark is the maximum event time seen so far minus a tolerance, say five seconds. When the watermark crosses a window's end, the event-time trigger fires that window. Events that show up after the watermark has passed their window are late; by default Flink drops them, but you can keep the window open with allowed lateness, or route late events to a side output so they are handled separately. The deep tradeoff is that the out-of-orderness tolerance trades latency against completeness: a larger value waits longer and captures more stragglers but adds delay, while a smaller value emits faster but drops more.

At the National Bank of India I used this exact pattern for real-time fraud detection. Transactions carry the real point-of-sale time, we keyed the stream by account, and applied one-minute tumbling event-time windows to count transactions per account per minute, because a burst in a single minute is a strong card-testing signal. We set a five-second bounded-out-of-orderness watermark so that slightly delayed mobile transactions still landed in the correct minute, and we routed genuinely late events to a quarantine side output rather than letting them corrupt an already-published count. We even watched the watermark lag as a Grafana metric, because if the watermark stops advancing it means a source partition went idle and windows would never fire. That combination of event-time windows and carefully tuned watermarks is what let us react within seconds while still being accurate about which minute each transaction truly belonged to.
